docs.text: Law and Economic Development Vorada Limjaroenrat Taipei School of Economics and Political Science 1 Course Information 1.1 General Course Info Course Title: Law and Economic Development Course Term: Spring 2026 Professor: Vorada Limjaroenrat (vorada@mx.nthu.edu.tw) Teaching Assistant: Heldha Oktavia Mega Puspita (heldha47@gmail.com) Office hour: Wednesday C08, 15.00-16.00. 1.2 Course Description This course explore the importance of judicial institutions, their impact on economic devel- opment, and how reforms in court systems can strengthen democracy, the rule of law, and economic growth. In doing so, it engages with some of the most fundamental questions in the social sciences: Why are some countries rich while others remain poor? Why do some nations embrace democracy while others persist under authoritarian rule? What constitutes a just society, and how can it be achieved? These questions have inspired generations of economists, political scientists, and legal scholars. In this course, we adopt a law and economics perspective to address these questions. First, it analyzes which types of judicial and legal institutions most effectively promote de- velopment and democratic accountability. Second, it delves into contemporary research on bias in the criminal justice system—e.g., political influence, gender bias, and racial discrimination—in shaping legal outcomes. Finally, it examines corruption, one of the central challenges in development economics, through the lens of the economics of crime. Students are expected to have a background in Microeconomics and Applied Economet- rics. 1.3 Course requirements and grading policies Group problem sets (30%) There will be three assignments during the course (posted after Week 3,7,&9). Students will work in the same pair throughout the semester. A group of three is permitted only if there is no other student available to form a pair. Students are not allowed to work individually on the group problem sets. 1 Discussion across groups is highly encouraged; however, each group must prepare and submit your own written solutions independently. Deadlines will be stated on each assign- ment. Late submission will not be accepted. Copying another group’s assignment, or submitting AI-generated work without full un- derstanding and the ability to explain it, will result in a failing grade for that assignment, with no opportunity for a retake. Seminar presentations (20%) There will be a case discussion and presentation in Week 2. Each presentation will last 15–20 minutes, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion. Students will sign up with the TA for a topic that interests them. In addition to the case presentation, each student must sign up (with the TA) to present at least 2-3 research papers during the course. These sessions will follow a research seminar format, with each paper presented for no more than 30 minutes, followed by 20 minutes of Q&A and discussion. Conceptual ideas from the presented papers may appear on the final exam. Students who are not presenting are strongly encouraged to read the assigned paper in advance and come prepared to actively participate in class discussion. I place strong emphasis on class discussion and participation and will actively facilitate debate and critical engagement during each session. Evaluation will follow a 360-degree format.  Presenters will be evaluated by both the professor and their classmates based on (i) the quality and clarity of the presentation and (ii) their ability to respond to questions and engage in discussion.  At the same time, audience members will be evaluated by the presenter based on (i) their level of active participation in discussions and Q&A sessions and (ii) the quality and thoughtfulness of their questions. After each presentation, the presenter will submit participation evaluations of their class- mates to the TA. Before the Final Project Presentation week, each student will submit evaluation grades for all presenters. An A+ grade must be supported by a clear and con- vincing justification. Final project & presentation (20%) Each student will choose one research paper from the presentation list (that is not chosen for weekly presentation, or is sign-up for final project before the presentation). A paper not included on the list may also be selected with prior approval.1 Students are expected to study 1It should be from either econ, political science, or law and economics journal. Econ journal: American Economic Review, Econometrica, Journal of Political Economy, Quarterly Journal of Economics, Review of Economic Studies, Review of Economics and Statistics, Journal of the European Economic Association, Economic Journal, American Economic Journal, Journal of Development Economics, World Development, Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, Journal of Labor Economics. 2 the chosen paper in-depth and complete a Final Projects which compose of two components: (i) Report Summary (approximately 2–5 pages); (ii) Elevator Pitch (1–2 pages). Grading will be based on (i) quality of the report 10%; (ii) elevator pitch 5%; (iii) presentation/Q&A 5%.  The report summary (approx. 2-5 pages) may be either qualitative (focusing on con- ceptual understanding and critical discussion) or quantitative (such as replicating part of the empirical analysis). Grading will be based on the depth of conceptual under- standing and the quality and clarity of the writing. Conducting additional analysis beyond the original paper’s scope or partial replication will earn bonus points.  The elevator pitch (approx. 1-2 pages) is a short research proposal that builds on the chosen paper. Students may propose an extension or improvement to the original study, address an unanswered question, or apply the methodology to a new context. The pitch should clearly articulate the research idea, explain its novelty and significance, and demonstrate its feasibility. In particular, students should discuss how they would test their assumptions, whether appropriate data are available, and what potential data sources could be used. Grading of the elevator pitch will be based on the originality of the idea, the clarity and importance of the research question, and the feasibility of the proposed study.  The final written report must be submitted before June 3, 2026, and late submissions will not be accepted. The final project will be presented in class on June 3, 2026 (Week 15), in an oral-exam format. During the presentation, students will be assessed on their understanding of both the selected research paper and their proposed extension. The purpose of this presentation is to ensure that students demonstrate a thorough understanding of their project and are able to communicate their ideas clearly and effectively. Final exam (30%) The final exam will be open-book and held in Week 16: June 10th, 2026. Political science journal: American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, The Journal of Politics, British Journal of Political Science, Annual Review of Political Science, European Journal of Political Research. docs.text: Public Economics and Development Seung-hun Lee Spring 2026 Web: https://seunghunlee918.github.io E-mail: seunghunlee@mx.nthu.edu.tw Class Hours: Tuesdays 9AM-12PM Office Hours: Tuesdays 2-4PM (Sign up here) Classroom: Innovative Incubation Hall A09 Office: Innovative Incubation Hall C06 1 Course Description Public economics addresses the roles of the government in the markets and their effects on the economy. It collects taxes and delivers essential public goods and services that private entities are not well-equipped to provide. It employs public workers managing and executing these services, often being a major employer in many countries. While taxes, public expenditures, and personnel are also crucial in the economic life of any country, developing countries face challenges that often do not exist in more developed countries. This course covers topics in public economics, focusing on the challenges goverments in middle- and low-income countries face. The course will begin by covering classical theories in optimal taxation. Then, the course will cover both applied theory and empirical papers highlight- ing challenges in collecting taxes, providing anti-poverty programs and other public services, and organizational capacity of public institutions in developing countries. By the end of the semester, students should be able to explain key concepts in public eco- nomics from both developed- and developing-country perspectives, critically evaluate theoreti- cal and empirical evidence in published papers, and develop original research ideas addressing open questions in the relevant literature. 2 Prerequisites • Micro/macroeconomics: The models discussed in the class are largely based on constrained optimization and principal-agent problems. Understanding how these problems are set up is crucial in absorbing the topics of this course. • Familiarity with statistical inference: The course involves assessing empirical evidence from developing countries. Understanding of statistical inference is a prerequisite for interpret- ing the findings. You must have taken or concurrently take quantitative methods course, with emphasis on regression analysis. 1 Public Economics and Development, Spring 2026 3 Lecture Materials and topics Lecture materials are composed of slides that summarize the textbooks and designated aca- demic journals articles for each topic, which are included in the latter half of this syllabus. The following textbooks are used throughout the semester. The slides covering key concepts in these textbooks will be uploaded on eeclass, so there is no need to purchase for the sake of this class. • Atkinson, A., and Stiglitz, J. [AS] (2015) Lectures on Public Economics, Princeton University Press • Besley, T., and Persson, T. [BP] (2011) Pillars of Prosperity, Princeton University Press • Hindriks, J., and Myles, G. D. [HM] (2013) Intermediate Public Economics, MIT Press The following books are other useful references for public and development economics. • (Undergraduate level) Gruber, J. (2022) Public Finance and Public Policy: Seventh edition, Worth Publishers • (Undergraduate level) Roland, G. (2014) Development Economics, Pearson • (Advanced level) Salanié, B., (2011) The Economics of Taxation: Second edition, MIT Press The following books are useful reference for empirical evaluation • Angrist, J., Pischke, J-S., (2009) Mostly Harmless Econometrics: An Empiricist’s Companion, Princeton University Press • Cameron, A. C., and Trivedi P. (2005) Microeconometrics: Methods and Applications, Cam- bridge University Press • Stock, J., and Watson, M. (2020) Introduction to Econometrics, Fourth edition, Pearson The topics covered in this course are as follows: 1. Stylized facts and classical theories on optimal taxation: Governments want to design tax systems that raise sufficient revenues while minimizing distortion in economic activities and maintaining fairness. How drastic are problems with inequality and welfare across countries and time? How are optimal tax collection and public goods provision achieved in developed countries? Why are these difficult to achieve in developing countries? 2. Fiscal capacity in developing countries: Tax collection in developing countries are different from that of developed countries. What theories and empirical evidence explain these dif- ferences? How does presence of large informal economy affect tax collection? How are developing countries adopting their tax struture to increase their fiscal capacities? 3. Anti-poverty programs and public service provision: Public goods, especially tranfers to poor households, are a huge part of government expenditures. How should these programs be designed: Should it be in cash or in-kind transfers? Should it be provided in the form of universal income or means-tested provisions? How should these spendings be targeted? 4. Organizational capacity of the state: Public sector is the largest employer in many countries, but are often inefficiently managed. How could the optimal allocation of authority across bureaucrats and managers be achieved? How can the public sector recruit capable and motivated individuals? How do the public sector incentivize and monitor the workers? 2/14 Public Economics and Development, Spring 2026 4 Grading policy and deadlines Referee report - 20% (Due: March 31st and May 19th) Students will write two referee reports on not-yet published papers, assuming that they are referees for a top field journals (e.g. Journal of Public Economics, and Journal of Development Eco- nomics). Each report includes a 200-word summary of the paper, a 1500-word assessment of its strengths and weaknesses, separating critical matters and minor issues in the paper. This assign- ment develops a framework for critically engaging with scholarly work. Students can refer to tips on writing reports found here and here. Papers that can be chosen for referee reports are as follows. Students must choose at least one paper from each topic. These papers will be uploaded on eeclass. Collaboration is not allowed for this assignment. Topic 1: Expansion of revenue-generating capacity in developing countries - Due: March 31st • Decet, D. “Organizing Fiscal Capacity” • Manwaring, P., and Regan T. “No shame in my name: Public disclosure and tax compliance in a low-capacity state” Topic 2: Organizational concerns in public service provision - Due: May 19th • Oré-Quispe, S. “Outcome- and Input-Based Incentives: Experimental Evidence from a Mu- nicipal Incentive Program in Peru” • Caloi, L., and Ciccarone, A. “Bonus or Budget? Equity-Efficiency Tradeoff in Performance- Based Transfers” Problem sets - 20% (Due: April 14th, May 12th, and June 9th) There will be 3 problem sets assigned throughout this semester. Each problem set is com- prised of questions testing the problem-solving skills on theoretical models and empirically repli- cating and extending an academic paper. For each student, only the two problem sets with the highest scores will be counted towards the grade. Collaboration is allowed, but each student must write and submit their own answers and codes, while identifying their collaborators. Theoretical model sections include questions asking students to solve the mathematical model, and to state the implications of the models in plain English. For some questions, the mod- els will be extended beyond what was discussed in class. For full credit, all derivation should be demonstrated without error and logical jumps. In the empirical sections of the problem set, students will be asked to write codes and pro- duce results that replicate and extend parts of the paper assigned for the problem set. Students should submit the codes they used as well as the answers (tables and figures) for full credit. 3/14 Public Economics and Development, Spring 2026 Research proposal and virtual paper - 30% (Due: April 28th and June 2nd) The task is to develop a viable plan for a paper that clearly motivates the research question, explains the background, data, and empirical strategy. If possible, some preliminary results that support the argument should be included in the paper. The aim of this exercise is to aid students in building up the papers that would be included in their thesis. As each student has different research ideas and specialities, students should frequently discuss their research idea with me or other professors at TSE. This task is composed of two parts. For the first part, you must submit a 2-page prelminary research proposal that outlines your research question, expected contribution, background, and potential data sources and empirical strategy. The deadline for this assignment is on April 28th. This task composes 10% of the final grade. The second part of the task is to amend and extend the research proposal to a virtual paper based on the comments on the first version of the proposal. The paper does not need to be complete-—a half-finished but original and exciting project is preferred over a complete yet uninteresting one. Depending on the progress and data availability, some students may be asked to produce preliminary results. The deadline for this portion of the assignment is June 2nd. Depending on enrollment, there may be a presentation on the paper on June 2nd. This task composes 20% of the final grade. The paper should be written in a scholarly article format. For instance: 1. Introduction: What is your research question? Why is it important from a scholarly or policy standpoint? 2. Literature review: What is the gap in the relevant literature? How are you filling that gap? 3. Background: What is the relevant information on the context that you are studying? 4. Data: What data source are you using or planning to use? Why should it be that dataset? 5. Empirical strategy: What statistical methods do you use? How do they allow for causal inference? What are the potential threats to that inference? 6. Preliminary results: What are the statistical relationships that you have found so far? 7. Mechanism and falsification tests: What factors may explain your main results? What are your plans to address potential factors that may nullify your findings? Final Exam (30%) - June 9th There will be a cumulative exam at the end of the semester. The questions will assess your understanding of the theoretical frameworks covered and ask you to connect an empirical find- ing—either provided in the exam or drawn from the reading list—to a relevant theory. Exact format of the exams (take-home or in-person) will be announced around May. 4/14 Public Economics and Development, Spring 2026 5 Rules on collaboration and AI usage Rules regarding collaboration Some assignments will allow for collaboration. In such case, (1) each student must write their own assignments, and (2) must clearly identify their collaborators. Rules regarding AI usage AI tools may be used for assistive purposes only—such as proofreading, grammar checking, and coding support. Using AI to generate complete assignments - papers, problem sets, and exams - is strictly prohibited. All submitted work must be original writing and analysis. To ensure oringinality, all submitted works will be subject to screening by AI detection program such as Turnitin. Any use of AI must be properly disclosed to the instructor. Violations will be treated as academic dishonesty and subject to disciplinary action under university policies. 6 Schedule and reading list Papers marked with an asterisks are going to be discussed in this class. I will usually cover 4-6 papers per week. These are the papers that are included in the final exams. Those without asterisks are still important and relevant papers that I leave for your own further reading. 6.1 Course Introduction and empirical analysis: Weeks 1-2 Course organization, and introduction to public economics in developing countries • *Bachas, Pierre, Anders Jensen, and Lucie Gardenne (2024), “Tax Equity in Low- and Middle- Income Countries", Journal of Economic Perspsectives, 38(1), 57-80. • *Besley, Timothy, and Maitreesh Ghatak (2006), “Public Goods and Economic Develop- ment", in Understanding Poverty, ed. by Abhijit Banerjee, Ronald Bénabou, and Dilip Mookher- jee, Oxford University Press, 295-315. • Besley, Timothy, and Torsten Persson (2013), “Taxation and Development", in Handbook of Public Economics, Volume 5, ed. by Alan J. Final-report (no more than 1000 words): 50% Course Description This course uses non-technical terms to explain various AI and the Internet of Things (IoT) technologies (AIoT) and then discusses the impact of AIoT applications on society, politics, and the economy. We are facing an era of tremendous changes, where our past thinking can no longer keep up. The only constant is that the speed of profound changes in thinking will only get faster. docs.text: Social Political Economy of Asia and Latin American Louis W. Goodman 1 Social Political Economy of Asia and Latin American Taipei School of Economics and Political Science National Tsing Hua University Spring 2026 Professor: Louis W. Goodman Office: Telephone: +1-202-390-5786 Email: goodman@american.edu Class Time: M 11:10 AM – 13:00 PM Office Hours: 10-11 AM &by appointment Assistant: Email: Course Description: The 21st century world is composed of evolving configurations of nations striving to achieve and sustain peace and prosperity and to produce public goods to support those goals. Understanding how these efforts take different forms in different regional and national contexts is critical for grasping both prospects for sustaining national economic and political development and for the nature of world politics. This course will examine such efforts in comparative context focusing on arrangements in Latin America and Asia. It will do so by examining economic, social, geographic, and political characteristics of Asian and Latin American nations in comparative context. Course Objectives: By taking this course with its focus on Asia and Latin America, students will have a better and clearer picture of the similarities & differences among regions in today’s international relations and socio-economic development. Their imagination will be stimulated, their knowledge will be expanded, their judgments deepened, their perspectives lengthened, and their ability to carry out independent thinking will be enhanced. Students who complete the course will be able to describe the specifics of economy, politics and society in Asia and Latin America nation-by-nation and in comparative context. In doing so they will gain a deeper understanding of economic, political and social change worldwide and will be able to relate the work of this course to their professional objectives. Learning Outcomes Gain Knowledge regarding specifics of Asia and Latin America’s regional and national geography, economy, politics and society. Understand how national and regional comparison enhances each student’s capacity for understanding economic, political, and social change world-wide. Identify issues central to the discussion of economic, political, and social change and how these issues are discussed publicly and in scholarly and practitioner literature Recognize how the capacity to carry out comparative analysis can relate to professional careers in development Experience how comparative economic, political, and social analysis can be presented in written, oral, and graphic formats. Create a professional memorandum discussing one or more issues important for developing understandings of economic, political, and social change relevant for professional careers. Social Political Economy of Asia and Latin American Louis W. Goodman 2 Course Requirements and Grading: Specific Assignments: 1.) A 2 page memo identifying your geographic interest(s) regarding Asia and Latin America plus regional comparative issues you find interesting with a 1 page appendix listing 4 relevant readings (15% course grade) + a brief professional resume (ungraded) (due Saturday February 28, 5 PM) 2.) A graphic depiction (photo, data table, cartoon, map) relating to your career- related regional comparative issue with 1 page maximum prose explanation (due Friday March 20 , 5 PM– prior to week 5 class) (15%) 3.) A power point report comparing an Asian and a Latin American country on some important aspect of social political economy) - 2 slides/30 words per slide maximum, no notes allowed (dates assigned week 3; reports weeks 10-13 ) Readings will be assigned by student presenters (20%) 4.) A final individual memo on a career-related Asia, Latin America or comparative topic (2 pages max) to a putative boss on a specific economic, political or social strategy or policy (topics approved by week 9; memos due Monday June 8 by 5 PM) (25%) 5.) Class participation: Students will be expected to come to class prepared to comment on the week’s readings and to bring personal observations from sources beyond the readings. Students anticipating missing a class will be required to write a one-page minimum essay on the assigned readings and submit it to the instructor at goodman@american.edu at least 24 hours prior to class. Students with unanticipated absences will be required to submit a minimum one page essay as soon as possible. (25%) • All papers are to be submitted online to goodman@american.edu and cc’d to Teaching assistant.edu • All papers are due on time and may be penalized for lateness. • Assignments can be turned in early and revised until the final date due • Be professional: proofread your papers carefully. • Number your pages; use one inch margins. • Provide a complete list of Works Cited at the end of your paper for all sources • Class presentations will be graded both on content and style/effectiveness of presentation At the end of the semester, your total points will be converted to a letter grade based on the following schema: A 95% and higher B+ 87-89.9% C+ 77-79.9% A- 90-94.9% B 83.5-86.9% C 73.5-76.9% B- 80-83.4% C- 70-73.4% An “A” means superior work, a “B” excellent work, a “C” satisfactory work, a “D” unsatisfactory and/or incomplete work, and an “F” below minimum-standard work. Social Political Economy of Asia and Latin American Louis W. Goodman 3 Weekly Summary of topics, assignments, readings Please note that students will be expected to come to class prepared to comment on the week’s readings and to bring personal observations from sources beyond the readings. Students missing a class are required to write a one-page minimum essay on the assigned readings and submit it to the instructor at goodman@american.edu Class 1: February 23 Core Course Concepts Course goals & Introductions – instructor and students Asia and Latin America – Basic data Elements of national political systems The evolving world order Readings: “Multipolar or multiplex? Learn the institutional details of intellectual property including patents, trademarks, new products, product inventions, invention awards, design awards, research lab, new drugs, band value, etc. 30% 20% 20% 20% 10% National Tsing Hua University College of Technology Management Course Syllabus 2. Exploration of the determinants of countries’ and firms’ performance in developing intangible assets and intellectual property 3. Learn empirical designs and tests for statistical inferences on the (causal) effects of economic policies, infrastructures, institutional environments on regional and corporate innovation. 課程說明 Course Description 1. This is a lecture-based course and will be taught in English. 2. Students will need to use English in their reports. 3. Students will need to attend online or in-person conferences hosted by Prof. Hsu, including “Taiwan Symposium on Innovation Economics and Entrepreneurship” ( https://oir.site.nthu.edu.tw/p/404-1487-164855.php), “ NTHU-UNSW-SMU Symposium on Sustainable Finance and Economics” ( https://oir.site.nthu.edu.tw/p/404-1487-225483.php), and AIEA monthly seminar ( https://www.aiea.org/0504) and write reports on presented papers – more details will be provided in “Grading” and “Course Schedule” 指定用書 Textbooks No textbook 參考書籍 References No references 教學方式 Teaching Approach 1. Lectures 2. Student/colleague presentations 3. Guess speaker presentations (online or in-person symposium and seminars) 評分標準 Grading 1. Attendance: 20% 2. Assignments: 80% (4 reports on presentations in symposium/seminar) 教學進度 Course Schedule National Tsing Hua University College of Technology Management Course Syllabus Prof. Hsu will host 3-4 online or in-person symposiums (all online: https://oir.site.nthu.edu.tw/p/404-1487-164855.php & https://oir.site.nthu.edu.tw/p/404-1487-225483.php) in this semester. Each symposium often runs from 9am to 4pm (5 to 7 hour long). Prof. Hsu will also host monthly AIEA seminar (https://www.aiea.org/0504) that runs at 9PM-10PM on Friday or 9AM-10AM on Saturday. These symposiums and seminars are part of the lectures. In special occasions, the instructor will give online lecture instead of in-person meeting Tentative weekly schedules (this will be updated, subject to the instructor’s schedule): • Feb. 26 • March. 5 • March 12 • March 19 • March 26 no lecture • April 2 • April 9 • April 16 • April 23 no lecture • April 30 • May 7 • May 14 • May 21 no lecture • May 28 • June 4 Some examples of the lectures all based on my lecture notes or research papers: 1. Tung (hanstung@ntu.edu.tw) 1 Course Design and Objectives This graduate course is designed as a Ph.D.-level overview of advanced topics in inter- national political economy. As Oxford Research Encyclopedias nicely puts it, ”The concept of international political economy (IPE) encompasses the intersection of politics and eco- nomics as goods, services, money, people, and ideas move across borders.” According to this definition, IPE deals with a wide array of topics ranging from international trade in goods and services, international financial transactions in the forms of foreign direct investment and foreign exchange rate determination to other related issues such as im- migration and international organizations. Among all these potential topics, we choose those that have received most scholarly attention in the recent five years and are worthy of our close scrutiny in this semester. Given its level, the course assumes that students have had some background knownledge of the IPE literature and won’t go over its tra- ditional theoies and models. Instead, we will only dicuss advanced topics and focus on new theoretical breakthroughs and empirical innovations. As a part of the PHD train- ing, you should criticaly read the methodological details of the assigned readings and aggressively find ways to make your unique contributions to the field. Requirements 1. Active Participation: Each student is expected to complete all the required reading each week and to contribute to the collective discussion. Keep such questions in mind as you read articles and books listed in the syllabus: • What are the central issues at stake in this literature? • What are the major arguments of the works under study? 1 • How do they relate to the debates in the field? • How valuable and viable is the theory or argument that each puts forth? • Which scholarly disputes have been resolved? • What good further work lies ahead? 2. Class Presentation: We will have presenters (the number depends on the enroll- ment) for each week between Week 2 and Week 14. In this 15-minute presentation, you should include: • Your understanding of what issues the selected articles and books are dealing with and how they solve these issues • Your suggestions for alternative solutions • Two questions for class discussion 3. A Research Proposal: Each student is also required to submit a research proposal on a topic of his/her own choice (Feel free to talk to me for some advice before you start writing.). In your proposal, you need to justify your choice of topic (i.e., why is it puzzling?), define your research question (e.g. what is the dependent variable of interest?), develop a theoretical argument and testable hypotheses (e.g. what is your explanation?), identify your data sources, and specify your methodology. Your research proposal should not be more than 10 pages, double-spaced, and use times font no smaller than 12 point. The due date of your research proposals is December 27, 2024. 4. A Final Project Presentation: Each student has to present his/her research proposal in front of the class in Weeks 15 or 16. docs.text: Institutions and Behavior Course Description This Ph.D. seminar explores the interplay between institutions and political behavior, broadly defined. While centered on institutional and behavioral approaches, the course is organized around major theoretical and empirical debates in comparative politics and political economy. We will examine how institutions—formal and informal—and the behavior of political elites and citizens jointly shape critical outcomes in the contemporary world, including democratization, populism, globalization, immigration, and democratic backsliding. By analyzing these phenomena through an integrated institutional-behavioral framework, the course seeks to illuminate fundamental questions: How do political institutions emerge, persist, and decay? What behavioral foundations sustain or undermine them? Through readings, discussions, and applied exercises, students will develop the conceptual and analytical tools necessary to engage with these enduring questions at the core of political science. docs.text: Quantitative Methods III Spring 2026 Prof. Ching-Fan Chung cfchung1@gmail.com The goal of this course is to help students to conduct an in-depth quantitative research using computers. The main theme is the empirical time-series data analysis with emphasis towards financial applications. Class teaching will be based on my own English class notes. You will also learn to use the programming language R (I will start from scratch, assuming you know nothing about it). This course is fairly inde- pendent of Quantitative Methods II but assumes you have thorough understanding of basic econometrics (specifically some knowledge of matrix algebra which is one of the foundations of advanced statistic and econometrics).You must have a personal computer (preferably with Windows, Mac users may have some difficulties in reading my digital notes). Because this course is computer-intensive, you will also need to learn how to leverage AI in learning and doing your empirical researches. The course grade will be based on your class reactions to my teaching (Bad! Bad ! Bad! if you never raise hand to respond to my casual questioning in the class) and a term paper that shows your ability to use R to go through the whole process from data analysis to in-depth explanations of your empirical results. ï Review of basic Ecnometrics and matrix algebra ï Review of R ï The univariate ARMA time-series model ï The multivariate VAR time-series model ï The GARCH model for univariate and multivariate conditional variances ï Financial data analysis and risk management ◦ Downloading and plotting financial data ◦ Measuring the performance of financial returns ◦ Returns calculations and backtesting ◦ Sharpe ratios ◦ CAPM ◦ Drawdowns ◦ Downside risks ◦ VaR, ES
